reason: The narrative's primary elite figures—King David and military commander Joab—are portrayed very unfavorably. David commits adultery with Bathsheba, then orchestrates the murder of her husband Uriah by sending him to die in battle. Joab executes these murderous orders. The prophet Nathan explicitly condemns David's actions as despicable violations of God's law, saying David has 'despised the word of the Lord' and committed theft, adultery, and murder. God announces severe judgment upon David's household as consequence. While Nathan (also elite, as a prophet) is portrayed favorably, his role reinforces the negative portrayal of elite figures—he serves as God's instrument to condemn their wickedness. The overall narrative presents the elite (particularly the king) as morally corrupt and subject to divine judgment.
